text.p: Campbell Soup Co results for the first quarter of fiscal 1996-1997 year show the company on track in its drive to boost sales and profits through brand development and restructuring, chief financial officer Basil Anderson said.
"The first quarter is clearly on track with making the targets we've set for ourselves for the year," Anderson told Reuters in an interview.
Anderson declined to comment on analyst estimates the firm will earn $3.62 a share for the fiscal year to July 1997.
He also said Campbell had recorded record cash margins of 23.6 percent in the quarter.
Anderson said Campbell has previously disclosed aims to show seven to eight percent annual sales growth over time.
First quarter sales of $2.05 billion were up three percent over a year earlier. The increase was six percent with sales from divested operations excluded.

Asked about possible targets for future divestments, Anderson declined to be specific. But he said the Godiva chocolate business, subject of some speculation as a divestiture candidate, and the Pepperidge Farm bakery businesses seem likely to continue contributing to results.

"Regrettably we can't say which businesses are for sale, but if you look at our business and you see how well Godiva has done and how well Pepperidge Farm is doing, you have to assume that those businesses will help to drive results in the future," he said.
Anderson said Campbell's new premium soup lines would be in full distribution by January and reception so far had been "terrific."
A line of frozen soups also would be in stores beginning in January, he said.

Low-fat soups also were selling well, he said. A new 98-percent fat-free mushroom soup had reached seventh place among Campbell's top selling soup varieties, while regular mushroom soup remained at number three, an indication the low-fat line was not cannibalizing sales, Anderson said. "It's additive," he said.

Anderson said a decline in international grocery earnings of 20 percent, and in sales of two percent in the division, reflected in part increased marketing spending to build soup brands in Asia and the United Kingdom international sales, and in part lower beef product sales due to concern over "mad cow" disease.
"In the U.K. and in Argentina people are very concerned about eating beef products because of that mad cow disease, so that's hurting sales, particularly out of Argentina," he said.
But he said overall soup volume rose a strong nine percent outside of the United States.
